name: Islamic Democracy
summary: Islamic democracy holds that Islamic values and democratic government are compatible: rulers are chosen and held accountable through elections and consultation (shura), while Islam remains a source of ethics, family values and legislation. Its mainstream is pragmatic, competes in multiparty politics and accepts electoral outcomes, rejects a clerical or caliphal state, and usually combines social conservatism with market-friendly economics.
scope: The moderate mainstream often called Muslim democracy: Rached Ghannouchi and Ennahda, Turkey's AKP, Hasan al-Turabi and Yusuf al-Qaradawi's shura-based reformism, as described by Vali Nasr. It excludes Maududi's theo-democracy, Qutbist and Salafi rejection of democracy, Iran's clerical system, and secularist Muslim reformers such as An-Na'im.

keyFigures.name: Rached Ghannouchi
keyFigures.role: Co-founder and leader of Tunisia's Ennahda, who declared its move from political Islam to Muslim democracy in 2016

sources.title: Islam and democracy
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Shura, sovereignty, sharia limits, minorities, thinkers (Asad, Ghannouchi, Qaradawi, Huwaidi), Pakistan, Indonesia, Libya

sources.author: Vali Nasr, Journal of Democracy 16(2), April 2005
sources.usedFor: Definition of Muslim democracy: electoral pragmatism, rejection of the sharia state, market-friendly middle-class base, comparison with Christian democracy

sources.title: Ennahda Movement
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Ennahda's positions on women, economy, secularism, homosexuality

universal-healthcare.rationale: Inferred from the social-welfare and Christian-democratic-style platforms Nasr describes and the zakat ethic; no source states a healthcare position.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Inferred from the centrist, welfare-minded platforms of Muslim democratic parties; no source addresses wage floors directly.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Nasr ties Muslim democracy to an independent bourgeoisie and pro-market liberalization (Ozal, AKP), and Ennahda is described as mildly economically liberal.

public-ownership.rationale: Parties are tied to the private sector and market liberalization, so broad nationalization is not their program; inferred, not stated.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Zakat and social justice favor redistribution but the business-friendly base resists steep taxes; adherents are split and sources are silent.

unions-good.rationale: No source gives a position; centre-right Muslim democratic parties vary between labor-friendly and business-friendly lines.

property-fundamental.rationale: Muslim democracy combines religious values with the economic interests of the middle classes, and Islamic law traditionally protects private property, though not as an absolute.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Not addressed by sources; pro-business orientation is balanced by Islamic social-justice ethics, so adherents are split.

cut-welfare.rationale: Inferred from the Christian-democratic-style social programs Nasr compares them to and zakat-based solidarity; no explicit source.

worker-ownership.rationale: Not a theme of these parties, which draw on private-sector middle classes; inferred.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Sources do not address it; Ennahda leaders were themselves surveilled and jailed under Ben Ali yet governed through security threats, so views are split.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Islamic moral teaching prohibits intoxicants and Islamist-democratic parties draw on that ethic, though they generally do not push enforcement hard.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Not addressed; blasphemy concerns push toward restrictions while democratic commitments push toward free speech, and adherents differ.

strong-leader.rationale: Shura and elected representation are the core of the position, and the movement was itself a victim of authoritarian strongmen.

state-harmful.rationale: The position is about building representative government under Islamic values; rejecting the state is alien to it.

limit-guns.rationale: No source addresses gun policy; inferred neutral.

empower-police-military.rationale: Nasr shows Muslim democrats defending the democratic process against military meddling, which implies wariness of expanding security forces.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Islamic sexual ethics forbid it and even liberal-leaning Muslim democrats like Ennahda uphold them in law.

decide-locally.rationale: No source states a view on subsidiarity versus centralism; inferred neutral.

rehabilitation.rationale: Islamic penal tradition stresses repentance and mercy, but no source addresses prison policy directly.

traditional-family.rationale: Nasr lists morality, the family and social relations as the Islamic values that Muslim democrats integrate into their platforms.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Ennahda figures have called homosexuality a perversion or supported keeping it criminalized, and no mainstream Muslim democratic party supports same-sex marriage.

abortion-legal.rationale: Conservative family and moral values are central to the platform; Islamic law permits early abortion in limited cases, so disagree rather than strongly.

more-religion-public.rationale: Muslim democrats want to harness Islam's ethical values in politics and public life without enshrining a religious state.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Not a topic in the sources; adherents have no common position.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Ennahda opposed inheritance equality on Quranic grounds, reflecting a view of gender roles grounded in revelation rather than construction.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Nasr describes these parties as nationalist-moderate and as expressing Muslim cultural values, which implies valuing national and religious traditions.

gradual-change.rationale: Nasr stresses pragmatism, compromise and practice over theory, and Muslim democrats are reformist rather than revolutionary.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Not addressed; no shared position among Muslim democratic parties.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Not addressed; adherents range from pro-UN to sovereigntist.

free-trade.rationale: Nasr links Muslim democracy to export-oriented private sectors integrated into the world economy, which implies support for open trade; the long-run-for-everyone claim is inferred.

nation-first.rationale: Muslim democratic parties are nationalist-moderate yet many also stress ummah solidarity; no firm answer.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Not addressed; adherents divide between support for intervening to protect Muslims and suspicion of Western interventions.

open-borders.rationale: No source addresses it; inferred from nationalist-moderate orientation.

limit-growth.rationale: The parties are growth-oriented and tied to business, so limiting growth is unlikely; inferred.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; Islamic stewardship ethics are invoked by some but there is no shared program.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Not addressed; neither endorsed nor rejected.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; inferred neutral.

revolution-justified.rationale: Muslim democrats work through elections and coalition-building and explicitly respect democratic bounds, in contrast to revolutionary Islamists.

experts-over-public.rationale: The shura principle and popular elections locate decisions in representative consultation, not expert rule.

central-planning.rationale: Muslim democracy is tied to private-sector middle classes and market liberalization, so a command economy is foreign to it.

socialized-markets.rationale: Not addressed; adherents accept markets without requiring worker or public ownership.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Islamic law fixes inheritance shares, and defenders resist state alteration of them, as seen in Ennahda's opposition to inheritance reform; heavy taxation is inferred to be unwelcome.

basic-income.rationale: Not addressed; zakat gives a welfare tradition but no stated view on unconditional income.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Muslim democracy embraces commerce and a market economy, so abolishing money and wage labor is far outside it.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Not addressed; some Islamic finance advocates are critical of central banking but the mainstream parties govern through central banks.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Not a theme of these parties, which favor competitive electoral and market politics.

one-party-rule.rationale: Muslim democrats compete in multiparty elections and respect democratic bounds win or lose; Nasr stresses competition among parties.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Islamic democrats range from republican (Ennahda) to supporters of constitutional monarchy as in Morocco's PJD; adherents are split.

democracy-best.rationale: Ghannouchi describes Tunisia as now a democracy and the movement's very label is Muslim democracy, accepting electoral outcomes win or lose.

direct-votes.rationale: The model is representative consultation; direct legislation by plebiscite is not a theme and sharia limits matters open to a vote.

workers-councils.rationale: Councils replacing parliaments are alien to a movement built on competitive parliamentary elections.

right-to-secede.rationale: Not addressed; the parties are state-nationalist and unity-minded.

natural-rulers.rationale: Shura and equality before God run against natural hierarchy of rulers, though some conservative strands accept scholarly guidance.

political-violence-never.rationale: Nasr contrasts Muslim democrats with violent extremists, but mainstream Islamic thought accepts resistance to occupation and just war, so this is split.

war-builds-character.rationale: Not addressed; jihad is framed as defense or duty, not as character-building, so mild disagreement is inferred.

separate-church-state.rationale: Ghannouchi separates religious and political activity organizationally yet keeps Islam as a reference point and rejects extreme secularism; strict separation is not accepted.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Divisions run deep: Libyan and Ghannouchi-style democrats want sharia as the main inspiration rather than sole source, while Nasr's Muslim democrats discount a sharia state.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Rule through accountable state institutions is central; privatizing courts and defense has no place.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Islamic democracy appeals to a religious community and citizenship, not ethnic exclusivity; Huwaidi and al-Bishri argued full citizenship for non-Muslims.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Muslim democrats unite middle and lower-middle classes around religious values and reject class-war framing.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Social justice and zakat are valued but equality of outcomes is not a stated goal; centre-right platforms.

civilizational-union.rationale: Pan-Islamic solidarity is common in Islamic political thought, but moderate Muslim democrats focus on national electoral politics, so only a weak agree is inferred.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Religious ethics of obligation and community are central; self-interest as a moral good runs against them though markets are accepted.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Islamic ethics stress duties but democrats also affirm rights; adherents are split.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Not addressed; Islam treats nature as creation for stewardship, not strictly intrinsic value.

limit-population.rationale: Pro-family values lean against state population limits; inferred.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: The movement is pro-development and tied to export-oriented industry, so this view is far from it.

human-enhancement.rationale: Not addressed; religious ethics lean cautious.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Not addressed; consultation by people makes handing government to algorithms unlikely.

restore-past-order.rationale: Nasr describes forward-looking pragmatic electoral politics rather than restorationism, unlike Islamists seeking a caliphate; inferred.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Nasr characterizes Muslim democrats as pragmatic and driven by practice over theory, willing to compromise to serve constituents.

direct-action.rationale: The movement works through elections and coalitions within democratic bounds.

means-match-ends.rationale: Nasr notes democratic means are adopted as legitimate and not as mere tactics, which fits the idea; the maxim itself is not stated.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Wholly foreign to a pro-development, commerce-friendly movement.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Zakat provides for the needy, but a general need-based distribution is not the stated economic model.

production-for-use.rationale: The platform supports private enterprise and profit, so production for use over profit is not their principle.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Muslim democracy represents the bourgeoisie and Islamic law permits trade profit, so profit-as-exploitation is rejected.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Contradicts commitment to competitive democratic elections.

collective-farming.rationale: Private property and private-sector orientation make collectivization unwelcome.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Not addressed; anti-imperialist sentiment exists but not a theory of capitalism's inevitable wars.

taxation-theft.rationale: Zakat is a religious duty collected for the community and Islamic governance rests on public revenue, so taxation as theft is rejected.

harm-principle.rationale: Muslim democrats accept moral legislation drawn from Islamic values, including limits on self-regarding acts like alcohol, per Nasr on stricter moral laws.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Islamic thought includes community and family rights alongside individual ones, and citizenship rights for minorities are group-recognised.

conscription.rationale: Not addressed; Muslim-majority states commonly conscript and no stated position.

exit-over-voice.rationale: The whole movement rests on voting and representation as the check on rulers, per shura and elections.

state-as-business.rationale: Not addressed; the state is a moral and consultative institution rather than a firm.

positive-liberty.rationale: Not addressed in sources; adherents split.

media-academia-power.rationale: Not addressed; secular media elites are often criticized but no firm view.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Islam's teaching of equality across races makes this view contrary to it.

organic-representation.rationale: The movement competes through political parties, which it treats as legitimate.

total-state.rationale: The model is representative and constrained government with civil liberties; totalitarian direction is the Islamist-authoritarian pattern Nasr contrasts them with.

national-rebirth.rationale: Revival of Muslim societies is a common theme, but radical rebirth from decadence is more Islamist than Muslim-democratic; split.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Not addressed; moderate electoral parties do not pursue expansion.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Elected representation replaces oaths of personal loyalty, though bay'a (pledge) has a role in classical theory.

bound-labor.rationale: Contradicts Islamic and modern norms of free labor.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Islamic thought affirms revealed truth rather than power-relative knowledge.

universal-morality.rationale: Islamic thought holds universal moral truths, though sourced in revelation as well as reason, so agree with caution.

single-common-good.rationale: Maslaha (public interest) points to a common good but Muslim democrats also accept competing interests in electoral politics.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: No source addresses it; most Muslim-majority Islamic parties oppose or are cool toward it.

school-vouchers.rationale: Not addressed; religious schooling concerns exist (Nasr on Turkey's religious schools) but no stated voucher view.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Inferred from the market-liberal, business-friendly orientation.

economic-freedom.rationale: Nasr links Muslim democracy to bourgeois independence from the state, which supports the idea; stated only indirectly.

rule-by-example.rationale: Law, elections and accountability are central; rulers' example alone is not enough.

national-self-determination.rationale: Popular sovereignty within sharia limits and national electoral politics imply self-government, as in Pakistan's Objectives Resolution delegating authority through the people.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Muslim democrats see faith as a source of values for politics, so reason as the only guide is rejected.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Not addressed; zakat tradition is community-wide.

class-collaboration.rationale: Nasr describes a unification of middle and lower-middle classes and a nexus of religious and secular drivers rather than class struggle.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Reverence for heritage is strong; sacrificing it is rejected.

dominated-front.rationale: Anti-Western common fronts appeal to some Islamists but moderate Muslim democrats like the AKP engage with the West; split.

workers-nation.rationale: The sources give no view on whether workers should organize nationally or internationally, and Muslim democrats stress the national electoral arena without an international-class framing.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Ennahda professes equal civil rights yet defended Quranic inheritance rules and conservative views; adherents split between equal participation and distinct roles.

ban-interest.rationale: Riba prohibition is classical, but Iran and others apply interest in practice and Muslim democratic parties govern within conventional finance; split.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Contrary to Islamic equality of believers across race.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Nasr treats the state as arena for compromise and competition, not ruling-class tool.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: No source addresses immigrant integration; Muslim democrats in the diaspora and at home differ on how far newcomers should adopt the dominant culture.

elite-replacement.rationale: A conspiracy theory not part of the ideology.

proportional-representation.rationale: Nasr's multiparty, coalition-building politics fits PR, and Ennahda and others use it, but no stated principle.

national-mission.rationale: Not addressed; some Islamic strands carry a da'wa mission but Muslim democrats focus on domestic politics.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Ennahda claims equal civil rights but resists reform citing the Quran, so adherents deny systematic male advantage as the organizing structure.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Contrary to Islamic ethics of human dignity and family.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Ennahda members suffered abuses under Ben Ali's regime and the movement stresses the rule of law, though source is indirect.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Muslim democrats back state promotion of moral and social programs, not a minimal state.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Contrary to Islamic teaching on equality.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Islam teaches equality of persons before God and full citizenship for non-Muslims was defended by Huwaidi and al-Bishri, though gender and religion differences in law are kept by some.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Foreign to the ideology, with a weak disagree because it is simply not relevant.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Islamic democrats generally uphold sharia-based family law, which differs by religion; a uniform code would conflict with that.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Not addressed; some conservative Muslim opinion supports limits on proselytizing, but democratic commitments protect religious freedom.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Nasr notes Muslim democratic parties sought to remove limits on Islamic schools and integrate religious values into public life.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Elected rule and consultation are the central claim; Jahangir argues people can be the source of state power within Islamic limits.

trade-surplus.rationale: Nasr's account links the movement to export-oriented business but never states a mercantilist aim, so adherents have no common position.

population-transfer.rationale: Contrary to the citizenship and pluralism that Muslim democrats defend.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Competition in politics and markets is accepted, but struggle between peoples is not a tenet.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Not addressed; Islamic law permits penalties and force within legal bounds.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Ennahda was banned and persecuted, which makes it wary of bans, yet democratic systems usually permit protective measures; adherents split.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: No stated position; Republican freedom is not part of the sources.

separated-powers.rationale: Representative institutions and constitutionalism are accepted, with Ghannouchi praising Tunisia's 2014 constitution limits; checks and balances are implied but not stated.

vanguard-party.rationale: Muslim democrats seek electoral support rather than a vanguard.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Islamic justice and zakat give priority to the poor, a shared principle in the moderate tradition.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Public housing sales are not a theme in Muslim democratic politics, and the sources record no stance.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Not addressed; business-friendly base but labor sympathy exist.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Not addressed; justice-based reasoning opposes blaming population.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Not addressed; pluralist citizenship arguments by Huwaidi and al-Bishri suggest rejection.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Elections and shura are the legitimate selection method.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Ennahda members suffered under emergency repression and the movement stresses constitutional limits, though security exceptions are accepted by some.

party-commands-army.rationale: Muslim democrats sought to keep the military out of politics and defend democratic civilian rule.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Citizenship timing is not discussed in the sources, and adherents do not share a view.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Not addressed; parties are electoral coalitions with varied internal discipline.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Not addressed; adherents divide on EU membership versus sovereignty; Turkey's AKP sought EU accession.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Not addressed; presidential and parliamentary models both occur.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Not applicable; Sunni Islam has no bishops.

clerical-rule.rationale: Nasr says Muslim democrats reject rule by sharia scholars as an Islamist state; Khomeini-style clerical rule is not their model, though some cite scholars' advisory role.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Contrary to national loyalty and to Islamic solidarity.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Muslim democrats accept moral legislation yet defend democratic pluralism; adherents split.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Elective, accountable rule suggests term limits, with Ghannouchi stepping back from clerical dominance; not directly stated.

recall-officials.rationale: Recall of elected officials is not discussed in the sources; accountability through elections is accepted but recall mechanisms are not a stated demand.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Not addressed; Turkey's AKP stayed in NATO.

people-in-arms.rationale: Not addressed; civilian rule over a professional military is the practice.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: No source takes a position on rural versus urban morality, though the movement's voters span both, with a strong urban middle-class base per Nasr.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Not addressed; pan-Islamic unity is a sentiment, not a stated program.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Islamic thought holds Islam's truth superior, though cultural diversity is accepted; inferred.

death-penalty.rationale: Classical sharia retains capital punishment for grave crimes, and Muslim democratic parties generally support it; however, Ennahda has been softer.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Conservative moral values oppose liberal sex education, but no source addresses it directly.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Not addressed; some Muslim democratic parties accommodate creationist views, others do not.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Nasr says these parties integrate Islamic moral teaching and have backed stricter moral laws.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Nationality law is not addressed in the sources, and the movement's emphasis on citizenship for all residents gives no clear lean.

minority-language-support.rationale: No source speaks to minority-language policy, which varies with local politics such as Kurdish issues in Turkey.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Not addressed; protection of minority religions is claimed but exemption doctrine is not stated.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Communal moral order and family values weigh against celebrating eccentricity.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Debt relief is not a documented position, although the Islamic ban on riba gives some sympathy; adherents govern states that repay debt.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: The sources record no view; Muslim democratic parties accept the existing property system and integration with the world economy.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Ennahda took part in Tunisia's post-2011 elected constituent assembly that wrote the 2014 constitution.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Muslim democrats stress competitive elections; Nasr ties political liberalization to the private sector's interest, not trade-offs.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Zakat and charity ethics support this, but no stated international position.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Defense doctrine is absent from the sources; Turkey's AKP stayed within NATO while some Muslim parties favor independent capability.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Not addressed; both parliamentary (Ennahda) and presidential (AKP later) are used.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Territorial compromise is not addressed in the sources, and adherents differ by country and conflict.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Islamic teaching holds property as a trust under social obligations such as zakat, and Muslim democrats combine property protection with social justice.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: A Marxist debate with no bearing on the sources; the movement takes no side.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Environmental regulation doctrine is not discussed in the sources, so no stance can be documented.

collective-defense.rationale: Alliance obligations are not addressed in the sources; AKP-led Turkey stayed in NATO but other adherents are sceptical of Western alliances.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Islamic political movements generally treat annexations without consent as unlawful, but sources do not state it.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Ghannouchi wants religion independent of political control and protected from being hostage to politicians, which opposes state subordination of religious institutions.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The sources do not address the head-of-state role; adherents live under both ceremonial monarchies and executive presidencies.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Secession is not addressed in the sources, and adherents differ depending on the state involved.

region-keeps-system.rationale: The one-country-two-systems idea is not discussed, and no source indicates a view.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Islam denies any divine status to rulers and shura limits power.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Tax-rate structure is not addressed in the sources; zakat is a flat-rate religious levy but that does not settle income-tax design.

character-from-environment.rationale: Islamic thought mixes innate nature (fitra) with upbringing, and the sources record no political stance.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Classical consensus (ijma) bound rulers and Muslim democrats hold rulers accountable to law and electorate.

space-expansion.rationale: Not addressed; not a priority for these parties.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Classical mixed-regime theory is not part of the sources; Muslim democrats back elected representation without a stated view on blended forms.

leader-cult.rationale: Islam condemns veneration of persons, and elected accountable leadership is the model.

equal-parenting.rationale: Custody rules are not discussed in the sources, and Islamic family law traditions differ on the point.

land-redistribution.rationale: Private property and a private-sector base make forced redistribution unlikely.

refugee-return.rationale: No source states it, but Islamic political movements broadly support refugees' return.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Classical law punishes apostasy, but Muslim democrats stress religious freedom and citizenship and generally do not seek enforcement; many reformists reject it.

women-must-cover.rationale: Ennahda supports equal civil rights for women and these parties do not generally seek compulsory covering, unlike Iran.

common-currency.rationale: The sources are silent on monetary union, and adherents have no shared view.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Pan-Turkic and pan-Arab union ideas are not part of the sources' account of moderate Muslim democrats, who focus on national electoral politics.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Minority self-governance is not addressed in the sources, so no stance is documented.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: The statement concerns diaspora strategy and is not addressed by the sources on Muslim democracy.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Contrary to a religious worldview of moral and divine guidance.

ban-cartels.rationale: Competition policy is not discussed in the sources; the movement favors markets but also anti-corruption and social justice.

no-bailouts.rationale: Bailout policy is absent from the sources; business-friendly governments often rescue firms while Islamic ethics criticize moral hazard, so views split.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Divisions: Muslim democrats accept majority rule within sharia limits, and Ghannouchi lauds constitutional limits, so adherents are split.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Ennahda put few women at top of lists yet supports equal rights; split.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Muslim democracy is tied to integration into the world economy.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Trade-treaty standards are not discussed in the sources, so no stance can be documented.

moral-incentives.rationale: The sources do not address work incentives, although religious duty and charity play a role in Muslim social ethics.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Contrary to electoral commitments and Nasr's distinction from violent extremists.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Elected representation and Islamic equality oppose hereditary privilege, though some adherents live under monarchies.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Not addressed; cultural identity emphasis suggests agreement.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Rejects colonial tutelage as a legacy of imperial domination.

patriotic-education.rationale: Nationalist-moderate parties generally favor national education; inferred.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Affirmative action is not addressed in the sources, and adherents have no shared position.

public-money-creation.rationale: Not addressed; Islamic finance critics of fractional reserve exist but no stated position.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Muslim democrats embrace market economy and see it adapting, but not explicitly stated.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Not addressed; Turkey's AKP pursued Ottoman-area influence but not a universal stance.

delink-world-market.rationale: Nasr links Muslim democracy to integration with the world economy.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Not addressed; a Marxist category foreign to these parties.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Equal citizenship for non-Muslims is argued by Muslim democratic thinkers, and Islamic equality opposes arbitrary discrimination.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Ghannouchi praises Tunisia's 2014 constitution for setting limits on both secular and religious extremism, which implies support for entrenched constitutional protections.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: The sources give no view on colonial border treaties, though anti-colonial sentiment is common among adherents.

elective-rulers.rationale: Elected rulers by consultation is central to the Muslim democratic claim; shura is read as supporting elected representation.

minority-veto.rationale: Majoritarian electoral procedure is accepted; individual veto is alien.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Classical consensus bound rulers and shura reading is a check on despotism, supporting accountability, though classical caution against rebellion remains.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Divine law limits legislative power per Asad and Pakistan's Objectives Resolution, so parliament is not supreme; split between sharia-limited and fully sovereign parliament.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Islamic teaching requires kindness to animals, though no source in the audit states it directly.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Islamic law permits use of animals for food with humane treatment.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Zakat and charity are duties of the wealthy toward the needy in Islamic ethics.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: The movement is defined by active participation in politics and elections.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: A Frankfurt-school style claim not addressed in the sources; adherents criticize secular mass media on moral grounds but not as pacification.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: The hegemony thesis is a Marxist idea with no counterpart in the sources.

native-born-offices.rationale: Equal citizenship is argued by Muslim democratic thinkers, so reserving offices by birth is not supported; inferred.

party-own-road.rationale: This concerns communist party relations and has no bearing on Muslim democratic parties.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Not addressed; trade integration is valued over aid dependence.

return-lost-territory.rationale: The sources record no demand for lost territory by Muslim democratic parties, and views vary by country.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Not addressed; citizen equality suggests disagreement.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Constitutional anti-fascism is a European concern not addressed in the sources on Muslim democracy.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: The comparison of fascism and communism is not discussed in the sources, so no stance is documented.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: A question of US historiography outside the scope of Muslim democratic thought.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: The sources record no view on contested monuments, and local cases vary widely.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: The sources do not address this; adherents stress family roles but have no stated program for men's disadvantage.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: Domestic violence policy is not addressed in the sources, and no shared position is documented.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Nasr and Ghannouchi describe a distinct Muslim democracy that fuses Islamic values with democratic institutions rather than copying Western secular liberalism.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Muslim democrats sought to defend democratic civilian politics against the military's role.

paid-care-work.rationale: The sources do not address pay for care work; the movement values the family but has no recorded program on wages for it.

filial-duty.rationale: Honoring parents is an explicit Islamic duty and part of family ethics.

office-by-exam.rationale: Examination-based recruitment is not discussed, and Muslim democrats rely on election and party appointment.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Not addressed; pro-trade orientation is balanced by nationalism.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Islamic law has talaq and khul, but political positions are not stated.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Imperative mandates are a council-democracy idea not addressed in the sources on parliamentary Muslim democratic parties.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Pension design is absent from the sources, so no stance is documented.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Private property orientation opposes community-only tenure.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Representative accountability is a core of shura-based government; inferred for budgets.

single-official-language.rationale: Language policy is not addressed in the sources and differs by country, for example Arabic in Tunisia and Turkish in Turkey.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: The sources give no view; adherents differ between pro-investment and nationalist positions.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Anti-discrimination doctrine on outcomes is not discussed in the sources.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Islamic ethics of moderation lean toward agreement, but not stated in sources.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: The sources do not address covert support for insurgents, and adherents differ depending on whose insurgency is at issue.

corporate-influence.rationale: Lobbying and campaign money are not discussed in the sources; anti-corruption themes exist but without a stance on corporate influence.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Not addressed; Ennahda and others have been both targets and users of foreign funding.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Family-values emphasis suggests support, but no explicit position.

residents-only-property.rationale: Local property-purchase limits are not addressed in the sources.

job-guarantee.rationale: Employer-of-last-resort schemes are not addressed in the sources, and market-friendly parties have not adopted them.

democratic-peace.rationale: The democratic-peace thesis is not discussed in the sources, and adherents have no common position.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Classical Islamic thought stresses obedience to legitimate rulers within law; inferred.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Nasr ties Muslim democracy to export-oriented private sectors integrated in the world economy, which points away from protection; inferred.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Not addressed; AKP-style governments mixed liberal markets with state-led projects, so adherents are split.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Muslim democracy represents middle and lower-middle class owners, and Islamic ethics favor wide distribution, but no source states it.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Ennahda and similar movements rose against corrupt secular-authoritarian elites, and Nasr cites corruption as a cause of governance failure; the populist framing is moderate.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: A socialist-state doctrine irrelevant to this ideology.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Not addressed; moderate electoral Muslim democrats do not press irredentist claims.

missingStatements.text: Elected legislatures should be bound by limits set by religious law.
missingStatements.rationale: Asad held that divine law limits what a community can legislate, and Pakistan's Objectives Resolution delegates sovereignty through the people within Islamic limits, though Nasr's Muslim democrats discount a sharia state.
missingStatements.declined: Captured by laws-from-scripture, where this audit answers 0 because adherents split on exactly this point.

missingStatements.text: Citizens of a minority religion should have full and equal rights in a state shaped by the majority religion.
missingStatements.rationale: Huwaidi and al-Bishri argued from Islamic texts for full citizenship of non-Muslims, a view contrasted with Maududi's tolerated-outsider model.

missingStatements.text: Religious parties should compete in elections on the same terms as secular parties and accept the results.
missingStatements.rationale: Nasr defines Muslim democrats by respect for democratic bounds win or lose, and Ghannouchi separated Ennahda's party politics from preaching.
missingStatements.declined: Covered by democracy-best and ban-extremist-parties; not a separate axis.

notes: Strands differ sharply: Maududi-style theo-democracy and Salafi rejection answer sharia and sovereignty statements very differently. Ennahda's 2016 move toward a non-religious party is more liberal than parties such as Indonesia's PKS or Morocco's PJD. Several answers on sharia-linked questions are split (0) because mainstream adherents disagree.
